exercises.title: The three cases of delete
exercises.task: Read Min, Max (one straight path: a loop) and Delete. Run deletes a leaf, a node with one child, a node with two children, then the root, and prints the tree after each.

exercises.title: Write Delete
exercises.task: Fill the three cases of Delete. Going down to the node is given; each call returns the new root of its subtree, and the parent reconnects itself.
hints: When you first wrote this in December, you found the parent with a separate search and changed parent.Left or parent.Right. That broke when the node to delete was the root itself. Returning the new subtree root avoids the parent entirely.
No child: return nil. One child: return that child. The parent's n.Left = Delete(…) does the rest.
Two children: copy the smallest key of the right subtree into n.Key, then delete that key from the right subtree: n.Right = Delete(n.Right, n.Key).

exercises.title: Acknowledged segments
exercises.task: A TCP sender keeps every segment it sent until the receiver confirms it, in case it must send it again. Here they are in a BST by sequence number. TCP acknowledgements are cumulative: "ACK t" means everything before t arrived. (TCP was described by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in 1974.) DeleteBelow removes every key strictly below t and returns the new root. Do not delete them one by one: whole subtrees can be dropped at once.
hints: If n.Key < t, the node and its whole left subtree are too old: the answer is DeleteBelow(n.Right, t).
Otherwise the node stays; only its left side can hold old keys: n.Left = DeleteBelow(n.Left, t).
Base case: an empty subtree stays empty.
